summary: The Amphillogiai (Ancient Greek: Ἀμφιλλογίαι, "Disputes") are the personified spirits of disagreement, contention, and ambiguous words in Greek mythology. They appear in Hesiod's Theogony among the brood of Eris, the goddess of strife, and are listed alongside her other offspring as abstract daimones embodying the discords that afflict mortal life. Like most of Eris's children, they are allegorical figures with no developed myth, cult, or narrative of their own beyond this genealogical catalogue.
etymology: The name derives from the Ancient Greek ἀμφιλογία (amphilogia), meaning "dispute," "contention," or "unclear/ambiguous words." It is a plural personification, treating disputes as a collective of spirits rather than a single deity.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: The Amphillogiai are counted among the children of Eris, the goddess of strife and discord. In Hesiod's account Eris bears her offspring alone, with no father named, just as her own mother Nyx (Night) produced children without a partner.

Their siblings form a catalogue of personified misfortunes: Ponos (Toil), Lethe (Forgetfulness), Limos (Famine), the Algea (Pains), the Hysminai (Combats), the Machai (Battles), the Phonoi (Murders), the Androktasiai (Manslaughters), the Neikea (Quarrels), the Pseudea (Lies), the Logoi (Tales), Dysnomia (Lawlessness), Ate (Delusion), and Horkos (Oath). The Amphillogiai stand within this group as the spirits of disputation and contentious speech.

sections.heading: Mythology
paragraphs: The Amphillogiai appear in Hesiod's Theogony (lines 226–232), within the genealogy of Nyx and Eris that catalogues the dark forces threatening human society. There they function as allegorical personifications rather than active characters: they embody the disagreements, lawsuits, and ambiguous words that breed conflict among people.

Beyond this listing they are not notably personified elsewhere in surviving Greek literature. They possess no independent narrative, no recorded cult, and no distinct iconography, serving instead as part of Hesiod's moral cosmology in which strife generates a chain of related evils.
